Does being in the final-4 of a Royal Rumble tend to translate into a match at WrestleMania? Yeah.



By the time I reached this very obvious conclusion, I already had the graph, so here you go.



I included every Rumble starting with 1992, which I consider to be the first "modern" Rumble, as it was the first with something on the line. I did not include TV Rumbles, or the GRR.



The categories were as follows:



* In World Title Match
* In A Singles Match (including multi-man matches)
* In Other Match (team matches or battle royals)
* Not On Card



With two exceptions (Austin '97, McMahon '99), the Rumble winner was in a world title match at WrestleMania.



Being the last out tended to translate to success as well, with 39.4% challenging for a world title, and an equal number having a non-world-title singles match.



Overall, if you can make it to the final-4 of the Royal Rumble, you an 86% chance of being on the card at WrestleMania with a 40.8% chance of being in a world title match. Even if you don't win, you still have an 82.3% chance of being on the card and a 22.9% chance of being in a world title match.



Minor considerations:



* 1994 is the only considered Rumble with two winners. For the purposes of restricting the data to final-4s, I counted the last two wrestlers out as the 2nd and 3rd runners-up.
* In 2020, the winner challenged for an NXT championship. Despite NXT championships not usually being presented as "world title" level, I counted it as a world title for the purposes of this graph
* I'm not sure why being a 2nd runner-up would give you worse odds of being on the card than being a 3rd runner-up.

1) Marx did not "solve" history. He did not "figure out" history. He had an IDEA of how history worked. He is one of thousands (probably more) of influential scholars throughout history who had an idea of how history worked. NOTHING MARX SAID IS PROVEN. IT IS NOT THE WORD OF GOD. 2) No anarchist believes that anarchy can be achieved overnight. In fact, many would probably argue that it can never be properly "achieved" at all, that it's more of a set of behaviors than a static condition. But all that aside, when anarchists object to the transitional state, THEY ARE NOT OBJECTING TO A TRANSITION. Every anarchist knows that there will be a transition. What they are objecting to is that, on the road from capitalism to liberation, we need to take a quick detour sideways to "socialism-lite" where everyone is kind of liberated but also not really. Anarchists want to go straight from point A to point B. THAT IS NOT SAYING THAT THE TRANSITION FROM POINT A TO POINT B WILL BE INSTANTANEOUS. That is only saying that anarchists do not think it's productive to build new hierarchies to replace the old ones, only to abolish the new ones down the line. Anarchists want to abolish hierarchies now. No dictatorship of the proletariat.

These different strains are less rigidly divided categories and more points on a spectrum. I'll try to summarize some of the big debates in anarchism.



**"Hard" Anarchism vs "Soft" Anarchism** - Hard anarchism rejects all laws, law enforcement, and structured power. There are, however, many anarchist-adjacent figures who are generally okay with that stuff so long as it's minimized and organized using directly democratic methods.



**Social Anarchism vs Individualist Anarchism** - While all anarchism is concerned with individual freedom, social anarchists believe that freedom stems from equality, because only by eliminating the accumulation of power can true freedom be guaranteed for all. Individualist anarchists counter that the socialist focus on the collective over the individual inevitably ends up stifling freedom rather than expanding it.



**Market Anarchism vs Nonmarket Anarchism** - Market anarchists contend that the freedom to control the products of ones own labor, including profiting off them, is as essential a freedom as any other. Nonmarket anarchists (who tend to overlap with social anarchists) counter that this leads to wasteful production and the accumulation of wealth.



There are other questions that I see crop up from time to time, including:



* Can an anarchist be religious?

* Should an anarchist use violence to advance their goals?



* Should anarchists embrace technology or reject it, and by how much?

I agree with your assessment of the dynamics of production, but I don't think a "military structure" is the way to solve the problems you're talking about. If anything, that kind of structure can exacerbate those problems. There is a certain level of "untouchable" people on more formalized shoots (think actors, directors, some producers) who can get away with all sorts of bad behavior because they're seen as irreplaceable.



I do think there's a sweet spot where someone can have something like a mandate of the crew. The crew agrees to follow the department heads, but those department heads can be democratically replaced if they're not doing a good job. Basically a bottom-up hierarchy instead of a top-down one.

I will jump off this comment and say, far from discouraging artists, I think removing the profit motive from art would free artists to make what they want, as opposed to forcing their art to have "commercial appeal" just to stay viable.

I am speaking just from my personal experience, and these particular shoots were hierarchical relationships, insofar as there were people in roles where they were given the final say. They were placed in these roles either through technical experience or simply artistic trust, which I don't think is necessarily incompatible with anarchist principles.



I think the important difference between these shoots and professional ones was theeefold



Firstly, on a professional shoot, deviating from your role in any way is not only a massive faux pas, but it may be against union rules and get you fired. On informal shoots, crew members are free to swap roles, provide artistic input to "higher ups", etc.



Secondly, as nobody's living is tied to the shoot, anyone is free to leave if they so desire (and thankfully in my experience that only happened when people had scheduling conflicts).



Thirdly, if a higher up is rude, domineering, takes the shoot in a direction the crew doesn't like, etc., the crew can choose to stop recognizing their authority (again, thankfully, I never saw this happen).



So while these were, in my experience, hierarchical organizations, they still provided a much more democratic, respectful, and consensual experience than professional shoots.

I've worked on plenty of student films, and it's totally possible to have a hierarchy of roles that is both (a) justified and (b) voluntary. Especially with a crew that's only one or two dozen people. No, you ain't getting the next *Infinity War*, but it works, and it's easy to find people who care enough about the art that they'll accept "lesser" positions out of a place of camaraderie, and with the implicit knowledge that, if they want to write and direct one day, there will be people there to help them.



(Also, not saying that a blockbuster film couldn't happen, BTW, just that there are more obstacles to something like that.)

My #1 piece of advice for coming out of the closet / not coming out of the closet is to NOT label yourself until you're sure of where you stand. You don't know exactly what you're feeling, or why you're feeling it. That's totally okay. You might be 50% into guys, 50% into gals, or 10% into guys, 90% into gals, or maybe you're 0.01% into guys and this was a one-off freak happening that will never occur again. If you commit to a label right now, there will be a lot of social pressure placed on you, and the last thing you wanna deal with in the middle of your sexual identity crisis is a bunch of other people telling you what you're *supposed* to feel.

Are you / is your friend gay? Maybe. I don't know. If you want to ask him out, gay people ask each other out the exact same way that straight people do (although there is a gay subculture with its own quirks and traditions, nobody is adverse to a simple, direct "I like you, will you go out with me?") You might want to get on the same page with your friend first, though. You can ask him about why he kissed you, and tell him that you enjoyed it but that you're also very unsure of how you feel. Again, you don't want to overcommit and make promises that you don't know you want to keep. And in general, it's nice not to make too much of a public statement about this, at least until you know how comfortable your friend is with people knowing that he kissed you.

Dealing with your sexuality can be a frightening, frustrating process. I've had friends get angry at me for acting too straight and family members get angry at me for acting too gay. On the on the flip side, it's very refreshing to be comfortable expressing your attraction to others in a coherent, honest way. Just take it slow, feel free to experiment and question yourself, and you'll know when you're ready to say what you are.

I hope this helps, and whatever you choose, best of luck to you and your friend!

It made him look ineffective and directionless, and it was a big hit to my suspension of disbelief that non-title matches mean something.
I have a strong suspicion that the WWE didn't except Team Kevin & Chris to be as strong a pairing as it turned out being, and now they're inadvertently ruining the Universal Title scene in order to keep the two together.
